title: Not a body (7.9–7.10)
hookLine: he learns to think of God as spirit and truth
tomorrow: if God isn't up in the sky, where did Augustine look next?

cards: A crayon drawing on a fridge: a big man with a white beard, sitting on a cloud just above the roof. Augustine carried a grown-up version of that drawing for a long time.
He's in Milan now, a celebrated speaker, and in his head God is something enormous, spread through all of space the way sunlight fills the air. Even God has to take up room. So how big is God?
Bigger than everything, he'd have said, and whatever doesn't take up room must be nothing at all. Then someone puts some books in his hands.

teach.h: A SPONGE IN AN ENDLESS SEA.
teach.b: First, the trap he describes. Anything without size felt like nothing to him. He even pictured all of creation as a sponge floating in a boundless sea, soaked through with God.
Huge, everywhere, and still a body. Second, the books.

They were books of the Platonists, he says, translated from Greek into Latin. In them he read, not in the same words but in substance, what the opening of John's Gospel says: in the beginning was the Word.
What he didn't find there, he says, was the Word made flesh. That part he would find elsewhere. But the books loosened the picture.
Third, the line that undoes it.
John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is a spirit; and they that adore him, must adore him in spirit and in truth." Spirit here isn't mist, a thinner kind of stuff.

teach.h: NOT BIG, NOT SMALL, NOT A BODY.
teach.b: It means not a body at all. Not big, not small, not here instead of there. Fourth, why that freed him.
He'd been trying to fit God into space, and no space was the right size.

One to tell a friend tonight: Augustine wrote down his own sponge-in-the-sea picture, so readers could see exactly what he had to unlearn. The fridge drawing isn't a crime. It just isn't where Augustine stopped.

how: The Catechism teaches that God is pure spirit, without a body. Catholics still pray with images, icons and statues, understanding them as pointing beyond themselves rather than showing God as he is.

o: God as light spread like sunlight through air
God as a body larger than the whole universe
God as spirit, with no size, place or shape

games.q: beyond the picture — tap the pairs.
p: a sponge soaked in an endless sea
the Word, but not the Word made flesh
not a thinner body: not a body at all

s: Augustine always thought of God as pure spirit
for a long time he pictured God as something vast, spread through space like sunlight through air.
in John's Gospel, spirit means God is made of something thin, like air
that's the popular picture. Augustine's turn is that spirit means not a body at all.
Augustine says the Platonists' books didn't give him the Word made flesh
he found the Word in the beginning there, he says, but not the Word made flesh.

games.q: your little brother asks why nobody can film God with a phone if God is everywhere. by Augustine's book seven, what do you say?
o: God isn't a body, so a camera isn't the right tool.
God is too far up, past the clouds, for a camera.
God is like an invisible gas that fills the room.
games.why: Augustine's breakthrough was that God isn't a vast body at all. John's Gospel: God is a spirit. No size, no place, nothing for a lens to catch.

practice: Close your eyes. Each time a picture of God forms, a sky, a light, a face, a size, let it go without arguing with it, and stay with the quiet underneath. If you pray, you can rest in John's words: in spirit and in truth.

wordCard.voice: Not a body. Augustine's turn in book seven: God isn't a vast thing spread through space, but spirit, with no size or place.

carryVoice: Beyond the picture: pictures can point to God, but they can't hold God. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: God is a spirit; and they that adore him, must adore him in spirit and in truth.
